title: Epitaph of Raqōš (JSNab 17) — Nabataean tomb inscription, Hegra (Mada'in Salih)
language_note: Mixed Nabataean Aramaic and Old Arabic, accompanied by a shorter Thamudic D inscription. One of the earliest attestations of Arabic embedded in a Nabataean-script legal text.

findspot_places.name: Hegra (Egra / Meda'in Salih)
findspot_places.note: Confirmed against the Pleiades places snapshot of 2026-08-10 by coordinate — 26.798, 37.952 — feature types 'settlement, cemetery', attested -330..2100. Note that Pleiades also holds 427224440, titled 'Erroneous Duplicate: Al-Hijr (Mada'in Salih)', at 26.792/37.961 — 700m away and marked by the publisher as wrong. It resolves and carries a plausible point; 814675 is the live record.

original_text_excerpt: [Nabataean script, transliterated: dnh qbrʾ dy ʿbd Kʿbw br Ḥrtt l-Rqwš brt ʿbdmnwtw ʾmh...] — see Wikipedia article for the two competing scholarly readings (original JS edition vs. O'Connor 1986 revision).
original_text_note: Transliteration given is a paraphrase reconstruction; pull the exact letter-by-letter transliteration from Healey, The Nabataean Tomb Inscriptions of Mada'in Salih (1993), during ingestion.
reference_translation: As for this grave/This is a grave, which Ka'b bar Haritat made for Raqash daughter of 'Abd-Manat, his mother. And she died in al-Hijr, year one-hundred-sixty-two, in the month of Tammuz. And may Mare 'Alma [the Lord of the World] curse him who alters this tomb or opens it, save for him whom he has begotten. And may he curse anyone who buries or exhumes anyone else in it.
translation_source: M. O'Connor's 1986 reading, as reproduced on Wikipedia (JSNab 17), building on Healey's editio.
reference_translation_note:
THIS ENGLISH IS ADAPTED FROM O'CONNOR'S, NOT COPIED FROM IT, and that is declared here on 2026-09-23 rather than corrected, because fifty-two archived quotations resolve into this field as it stands. Measured against O'Connor's translation as https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSNab_17 prints it: the diacritics are dropped, the ʿayn written as a plain apostrophe; 'berat' is rendered 'daughter'; the gloss '[the Lord of the World]' is added after the god's name; the editor's parenthetical insertions and the alternative '/his progeny' are dropped; 'open' becomes 'opens'; and the closing curse is condensed. The sense is O'Connor's and the wording is an adaptation of it.

LANGUAGE RECODED 2026-09-23, S9: this record was curated with `xna` (Ancient North Arabian) for a Nabataean Aramaic epitaph with Old Arabic in it, and now declares `arc` and `arb`. The archive keeps the `xna` it recorded; the page reads it through ARCHIVED_LANG_RECODED.
notes: Notable for the epithet 'Lord of the World' (possibly monotheistic) and for mixing Aramaic and Arabic in a dated (267 CE) legal-funerary text — useful both as a language-contact data point and as a stress-test for cross-lingual retrieval given the two competing scholarly transliterations.
